[[Bill English]] | predecessor3 = [[Paula Bennett]] | successor3 = [[Carmel Sepuloni]] | order4 = 44th [[Minister of Education (New Zealand)|Minister of Education]] | term_start4 = 19 November 2008 | term_end4 = 25 November 2011 | prime_minister4 = [[John Key]] | predecessor4 = [[Chris Carter (New Zealand politician)|Chris Carter]] | successor4 = [[Hekia Parata]] | order5 = Minister for Tertiary Education | term_start5 = 19 November 2008 | term_end5 = 27 January 2010{{cite news|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10622389|title=John Key announces Cabinet reshuffle|date=26 January 2010|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|access-date=26 January 2010}} | prime_minister5 = [[John Key]] | predecessor5 = [[Pete Hodgson]] | successor5 = [[Steven Joyce]] | constituency_MP6 = [[East Coast (New Zealand electorate)|East Coast]] | parliament6 = New Zealand | majority6 = 6,413 | predecessor6 = [[Janet Mackey]] | successor6 = [[Kiri Allan]] | term_start6 = 17 September 2005 | term_end6 = 17 October 2020 | constituency_MP7 = [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] [[list MP|list]] | parliament7 = New Zealand | term_start7 = 27 November 1999 | term_end7 = 27 July 2002 | birth_name = Anne Merrilyn Hicks | birth_date = {{birth date and age|df=yes|1953|03|1}} | birth_place = [[Wellington]], New Zealand | death_date = | death_place = | spouse = {{marriage|Allan Hunt Tolley|1973}} | party = [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] | relations = | children = Three | alma_mater = | occupation = Hotelier, Local Government | profession = | signature = | website = {{URL|http://annetolley.co.nz/}} | footnotes = }} '''Anne Merrilyn Tolley''' {{post-nominals|country=NZL|JP|size=85%}} (née '''Hicks'''; born 1 March 1953) is a New Zealand politician. Tolley was elected as a member of the [[Napier City Council]] in 1986 and served as deputy mayor from 1989 until 1995. In 1999 she was elected to Parliament as a [[list MP]] representing the [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]]. She was unseated in 2002 but returned in 2005 as the new [[East Coast (New Zealand electorate)|East Coast]] MP. Between 2008 and 2017 she was a senior minister in the [[Fifth National Government of New Zealand|Fifth National Government]], holding the offices of [[Minister of Education (New Zealand)|Minister of Education]], [[Minister for Social Development (New Zealand)|Minister of Social Development]], [[Minister of Corrections (New Zealand)|Minister of Corrections]], [[Minister of Police (New Zealand)|Minister of Police]] and [[Minister of Local Government (New Zealand)|Minister of Local Government]]. She established [[Oranga Tamariki]] and was the first [[Minister for Children (New Zealand)|Minister for Children]] from 2016 to 2017. She was [[Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives#Deputies|Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives]] from 2017 to 2020. In 2021 she was appointed chair of the commission overseeing the [[Tauranga City Council]].{{cite web|url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/commissioners-appointed-tauranga-city-council|title=Commissioners appointed to Tauranga City Council|access-date=2022-04-14|date=2 February 2021}} ==Early life and family== Tolley was born in [[Wellington]] on 1 March 1953, the daughter of Mary Margaret Hicks (née Norris) and her husband Ronald James Hicks. She was educated at Colenso High School (now [[William Colenso College]]) in [[Napier, New Zealand|Napier]], and spent time as a [[Rotary Youth Exchange|Rotary exchange student]] in [[Allentown, Pennsylvania]], United States. She went on to gain a diploma in computer programming. In 1973 she married Allan Hunt Tolley, and the couple had three children.{{cite journal |editor-last=Taylor |editor-first=Alister |title=New Zealand Who's Who Aotearoa 2001 |journal=New Zealand Who's Who, Aotearoa |year=2001 |publisher=Alister Taylor Publishers |location=Auckland |issn=1172-9813}} With her husband, Tolley ran a boutique hotel in Napier.{{Cite news|last=Laing|first=Doug|date=2020-07-03|title=The shoulder tap that could have turned National MP Anne Tolley to Labour|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12344312|access-date=2020-07-24|issn=1170-0777}} ==Local government== In 1986 Tolley was elected as a member of the Napier City Council and remained in that role until 1995. She served as deputy [[Mayor of Napier (New Zealand)|mayor of Napier]] between 1989 and 1995, and was an elected member of the [[Hawke's Bay Region|Hawke's Bay Regional Council]] from 1989 to 1992. She has been a [[Justice of the peace#New Zealand|Justice of the Peace]] since 1989. While on Napier City Council, Tolley was involved in the establishment of a [[local-authority trading enterprise]] to run [[Marineland of New Zealand|Marineland]] and the [[National Aquarium of New Zealand|Napier Aquarium]], the Emerson Street redevelopment project, and the redevelopment of [[McLean Park]]. She sought re-election in the 1995 local elections, but was defeated. ==Member of Parliament== {{NZ parlbox header|align=left}} {{NZ parlbox|term=46th|start={{NZ election link year|1999}}|end=2002|electorate=List|list=20|party=New Zealand National Party}} {{NZ parlbox break}} {{NZ parlbox|term=48th|start={{NZ election link year|2005}}|end=2008|electorate={{NZ electorate link|East Coast}}|list=43|party=New Zealand National Party}} {{NZ parlbox|term=49th|start={{NZ election link year|2008}}|end=2011|electorate=East Coast|list=10|party=New Zealand National Party}} {{NZ parlbox|term=50th|start={{NZ election link year|2011}}|end=2014|electorate=East Coast|list=8|party=New Zealand National Party}} {{NZ parlbox|term=51st|start={{NZ election link year|2014}}|end=2017|electorate=East Coast|list=12|party=New Zealand National Party}} {{NZ parlbox|term=52nd|start={{NZ election link year|2017}}|end=2020|electorate=East Coast|list=11|party=New Zealand National Party}} {{End}} An independent on the Napier City Council, Tolley was encouraged to join the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] by incumbent [[Napier (New Zealand electorate)|Napier]] MP [[Geoff Braybrooke]] but declined, instead joining the National Party. She was interested in being a candidate for National at the [[1996 New Zealand general election|1996 general election]], but had not been a member of the party for long enough. She challenged Braybrooke for the Napier seat in [[1999 New Zealand general election|1999]]. While unsuccessful in that contest, Tolley was elected as a [[list MP]]. In her first term, Tolley sat on the governance and administration committee and served as the National Party spokesperson for early childhood education and women's affairs.{{cite web |title=Tolley, Anne |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/tolley-anne/ |access-date=4 May 2024 |website=New Zealand Parliament}} In 2000, her members bill—the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Prohibition of Child Pornography) Amendment Bill—was introduced.{{cite web |date=26 March 2024 |title=Still No Action On Bill To Prohibit Child Porn |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0010/S00084/still-no-action-on-bill-to-prohibit-child-porn.htm |access-date=4 May 2024 |website=Scoop News}} The bill responded to, and sought to overturn, the Court of Appeal's decision on ''Moonen v Film and Literature Board of Review'', which had found that the right to freedom of expression in the [[New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990]] held even in the [[Film and Literature Board of Review]]'s consideration of photographs depicting children in sexualised poses.{{cite web |date=26 March 2024 |title=Still No Action On Bill To Prohibit Child Porn |url=https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0010/S00084/still-no-action-on-bill-to-prohibit-child-porn.htm |access-date=5 May 2024 |website=Scoop News}} The bill was eventually voted down because the government did not consider ''Moonen'' to sanction child pornography. Issues around censorship were progressed soon after through an inquiry into the [[Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993]] and a government amendment passed in 2005.{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=David |date=December 2002 |title=Censorship In New Zealand: The Policy Challenges of New Technology |url=https://www.msd.govt.nz/documents/about-msd-and-our-work/publications-resources/journals-and-magazines/social-policy-journal/spj19/19-pages1-13.pdf |journal=Social Policy Journal of New Zealand |issue=19}}{{cite web |title=Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Amendment Bill |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/47HansD_20050216_00001132/films-videos-and-publications-classification-amendment |access-date=4 May 2024 |website=New Zealand Parliament}} In the [[2002 New Zealand general election|2002 election]], she unsuccessfully contested the Napier seat against Braybrooke's successor, [[Russell Fairbrother]]. Along with many other National MPs, Tolley did not escape the collapse of the party's vote that year, and so did not return to Parliament as a list MP.{{cite news|url=http://www.newshub.co.nz/general/candidate-profile-anne-tolley-2011102014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221162446/http://www.newshub.co.nz/general/candidate-profile-anne-tolley-2011102014 |url-status=dead |archive-date=21 December 2016 |title=Candidate profile: Anne Tolley |newspaper=[[Newshub]] |date=2011-10-20 |access-date=2017-07-17}} She did return at the [[2005 New Zealand general election|2005 general election]], having won the [[East Coast (New Zealand electorate)|East Coast]] electorate over Labour candidate [[Moana Mackey]], daughter of the previous East Coast MP [[Janet Mackey]].{{cite web|url=https://www.parliament.nz/resource/mi-nz/00PLSocEP05121/cde0b76e9906c164721d1dafe0033861f0cf73ab |title=Electorate Profile East Coast |date=October 2005 |website=Parliament.nz |access-date=2017-07-17}} She held the electorate at the four subsequent elections. She served as the first woman National Party [[Whip (politics)|whip]] from December 2006 until February 2008 when she became the party's education spokesperson.{{cite news|url=http://www.newshub.co.nz/nznews/katherine-rich-puts-family-before-politics-in-her-decision-to-stand-down-2008021318 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161222000333/http://www.newshub.co.nz/nznews/katherine-rich-puts-family-before-politics-in-her-decision-to-stand-down-2008021318 |url-status=dead |archive-date=22 December 2016 |title=Katherine Rich puts family before politics in her decision to stand down |newspaper=[[Newshub]] |date=2008-02-13 |access-date=2017-07-17}}{{cite web |last=Jones |first=Charlotte |date=30 June 2020 |title=Anne Tolley reflects on her work in politics as she bows out |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/420197/anne-tolley-reflects-on-her-work-in-politics-as-she-bows-out |access-date=4 May 2024 |website=[[RNZ]] }} When National won the 2008 general election, she became the first woman [[Minister of Education (New Zealand)|Minister of Education]]. She continued in senior roles in the [[Fifth National Government of New Zealand|Fifth National Government]] until its defeat in 2017 and thereafter became [[Deputy Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives|Deputy Speaker]]. In that role, she chaired a cross-party steering group steering group to develop a parliamentary code of conduct, as an outcome of an independent review into bullying and harassment in the parliamentary workplace.{{Cite web |date=2020-07-07 |title=Bullying and harassment in Parliament – one year on |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/page/bullying-and-harassment-in-parliament-one-year-on |access-date=2020-07-24 |website=Newsroom}} This occurred after interrupting Youth MP Lily Dorrance's speech at the [[New Zealand Youth Parliament#9th Youth Parliament (2019)|2022 Youth Parliament]], leaving Dorrance "humiliated", which Tolley said made her "all the more aware of the issues".{{Cite web |date=2019-07-17 |title=Tolley chairing group to fight bullying in Parliament |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/deputy-speaker-anne-tolley-chairing-group-to-fight-bullying-in-parliament/FBWJVYUZINBOTWQYWBJQ2NODAA/ |access-date=2025-05-15 |website=NZ Herald |language=en-NZ}} At the end of 2019, Tolley declared her intention to run as a list-only candidate in the 2020 general election in hope of being able to be appointed [[Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives|Speaker of the House]] if National were able to form a government.{{Cite web |date=2019-12-19 |title=Anne Tolley to go list only in 2020, citing ambitions to be Speaker |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/118360382/anne-tolley-to-go-list-only-in-2020-citing-ambitions-to-be-speaker |access-date=2020-07-24 |website=Stuff}} She was succeeded as National's candidate for the East Coast electorate by [[Rotorua District Council]]lor [[Tania Tapsell]].{{Cite news |last=Conchie |first=Sandra |date=2020-06-06 |title=Rotorua Lakes councillor Tania Tapsell selected to be National Party candidate for East Coast |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/rotorua-daily-post/news/article.cfm?c_id=1503438&objectid=12337732 |access-date=2020-07-24 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |issn=1170-0777}} However, in June 2020, with National polling poorly,{{Cite web |title=Tolley says it is time for family |url=http://www.gisborneherald.co.nz/local-news/20200629/tolley-says-it-time-for-the-family/ |access-date=2020-07-24 |website=www.gisborneherald.co.nz}} Tolley announced that she would instead retire |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300043727/anne-tolley-to-retire-from-parliament-this-year |access-date=27 June 2020 |publisher=Stuff}} She gave her valedictory statement on 23 July |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12350550 |access-date=2020-07-24 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |issn=1170-0777}}{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Charlotte |access-date=2020-07-24 |website=[[RNZ]] }} == Minister in the Fifth National Government == ===Minister of Education: 2008–2011=== The National Party formed a [[Fifth National Government of New Zealand|government]] after the [[2008 New Zealand general election|2008 general election]] and Tolley was appointed [[Minister of Education (New Zealand)|Minister of Education]], the first woman to hold that position. The key policy introduced during her term was introduction of the National Standards programme that measured children's progress against the curriculum in reading, writing and mathematics, in order to increase schools' accountability.[http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10767804 Editorial: Trust parents with the facts about schools], NZ Herald 22 November 2011 The programme was opposed by many teachers and school principals, some of whom refused to implement the standards.{{cite web |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10767903 |title=Principals reject education policy – National – NZ Herald News |website=www.nzherald.co.nz |access-date=26 January 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130223003750/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10767903 |archive-date=23 February 2013 |url-status=dead}} In January 2010, Tolley's responsibilities for tertiary education were reassigned to [[Steven Joyce]], with Prime Minister [[John Key]] stating that this would allow Tolley to focus on the implementation of national standards.{{Cite news|last=Young|first=Audrey|date=2010-01-26|title=Tolley relieved of portfolio to focus on national standards|work=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10622467|access-date=2020-07-24|issn=1170-0777}} In June 2010, Tolley expressed concerns about a Parliamentary Library research paper that was critical of National Standards, calling it "unprofessional", "highly political" and so biased it could have been written by the union opposing the policy. Such papers are required by the Parliamentary Library to be politically neutral.{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10655408 |title=Tolley upset at paper on standards |author=Young, Audrey |date=30 June 2010 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |access-date=16 September 2011}} A month later the New Zealand Principals Federation voted to support regional associations which boycotted training for National Standards. Tolley reminded principals that in her view it would be quicker and give better results to contact herself or the Ministry of Education with concerns about the changes, than to speak through the media.{{cite web |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10655999 |title=Minister warns principals against speaking out about standards – National – NZ Herald News |website=www.nzherald.co.nz |access-date=26 January 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130223004422/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10655999 |archive-date=23 February 2013 |url-status=dead}} The stand-off between Tolley and teachers was embarrassing for the Government and resulted in Cabinet changes after National was re-elected in November 2011.{{cite news| url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10772885 | work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | title=Women move up the Govt ranks | date=13 December 2011}} [[Hekia Parata]] was made Education Minister while Tolley was demoted in the Cabinet rankings, becoming Minister of Corrections and Police,{{cite news| url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10772717 | work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | first=Amelia | last=Romanos | title=Boost for women in new Cabinet | date=12 December 2011}} succeeding [[Judith Collins]] who was promoted to Minister of Justice.{{cite news| url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/news/article.cfm?c_id=3&objectid=10719004 | work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] | title=Power hands over SOE portfolio | date=13 April 2011}} ===Minister of Police and Minister of Corrections: 2011–2014=== In March 2012, one of her first major announcements as the Minister of Corrections was the proposed closure of the old prisons in Wellington and New Plymouth. She also said that a number of older units at Arohata, Rolleston, Rangipo and Waikeria prisons would close.{{cite web |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10794029 |title=Minister defends prison closure plans – National – NZ Herald News |website=www.nzherald.co.nz |access-date=26 January 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130112044314/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10794029 |archive-date=12 January 2013 |url-status=dead}} Later that year, the Government awarded a 25-year contract to Serco to build a 960-bed prison at [[Wiri]], South Auckland, at a cost of NZ$900 million.{{cite press release|last=Clendon |first=David |author-link=David Clendon |title=$900 million for empty beds |date=21 June 2012 |publisher=[[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]] |location=Wellington |url=http://www.greens.org.nz/press-releases/900-million-empty-beds |access-date=29 December 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130210183642/http://www.greens.org.nz/press-releases/900-million-empty-beds |archive-date=10 February 2013 }}{{cite news |title=Minister defends prison closure plans |url= http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10794029 |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |author=APNZ |author-link=APNZ |date=23 March 2012 |access-date=29 December 2012}} Tolley attended a sod-turning ceremony at the site of the new prison Wiri in September 2012.{{Cite web |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10835281 |title=Construction begins on $300m prison |date=7 March 2012 |access-date=20 September 2012 |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20120920055306/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10835281 |archive-date=20 September 2012 |url-status=live }} In June 2012, Tolley as Police Minister was responsible for crushing the first "[[boy racer]]" car under the [[Vehicle Confiscation and Seizure Bill (New Zealand)|Vehicle Confiscation and Seizure Act]].{{Cite web|date=2012-06-21|title=Boy racers mourn first crushed car|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/crime/7145120/Boy-racers-mourn-first-crushed-car|access-date=2020-07-24|website=Stuff}} === Minister of Social Development and Minister for Children: 2014–2017 === When National was returned to government after the [[2014 New Zealand general election|2014 general election]], Tolley succeeded [[Paula Bennett]] as [[Minister for Social Development (New Zealand)|Minister of Social Development]]. A key achievement during this term was reforming the [[Child, Youth and Family (New Zealand)|Child, Youth and Family]] service within the [[Ministry of Social Development (New Zealand)|Ministry of Social Development]] into a standalone agency, [[Oranga Tamariki|Oranga Tamariki, the Ministry for Children]], after a Children's Commissioner report in 2015 found that the government had failed children in state care.{{cite news |last1=Kenny |first1=Katie |title=Faces of Innocents: CYF to be shut down and replaced by a new ministry |url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/faces-of-innocents/82526149/faces-of-innocents-cyf-to-be-shut-down-and-replaced-by-a-new-ministry |access-date=18 June 2019 |publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=28 July 2016}} From September to December 2016, Tolley had an additional appointment as Minister for Youth. On 20 December 2016 she became the Minister for Children and the [[Minister of Local Government (New Zealand)|Minister of Local Government]] and held these roles, along with Minister of Social Development, until the Government was defeated at the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 general election]].{{cite web|url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/document/51MP1811/tolley-anne |title=Tolley, Anne – New Zealand Parliament |website=Parliament.nz |date=2017-04-07 |access-date=2017-07-17}} Along with former state services minister Paula Bennett, Tolley was accused by [[New Zealand First]] party leader [[Winston Peters]] in 2017 of leaking information about his incorrectly filed superannuation application.{{Cite web|date=2019-11-14|title=Bennett, Tolley avoid financial damages in Peters privacy case|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/403234/bennett-tolley-avoid-financial-damages-in-peters-privacy-case|access-date=2020-07-24|website=[[RNZ]] }} Tolley admitted having told her sister of the situation before it was reported by media, but was not found to have alerted media.{{Cite web|date=2019-11-07|title=Anne Tolley admits 'outburst' in Winston Peters superannuation case|url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/402745/anne-tolley-admits-outburst-in-winston-peters-superannuation-case|access-date=2020-07-24|website=[[RNZ]] }} ==Tauranga City Council== On 9 February 2021, the Minister of Local Government appointed a Crown Commission to oversee all of [[Tauranga City Council]]'s governance responsibilities {{Cite web|title=Our Council – Tauranga City Council|url=https://www.tauranga.govt.nz/council/about-your-council/our-council|access-date=2021-02-23|website=www.tauranga.govt.nz}} (with all existing elected members being discharged). Tolley was appointed commission chair.{{Cite web|title=Commissioners – Tauranga City Council|url=https://www.tauranga.govt.nz/council/about-your-council/commissioners|access-date=2021-02-23|website=www.tauranga.govt.nz}} ==Health== It emerged in 2010 that Tolley had undergone gastric bypass (stomach stapling) surgery in order to lose weight.{{cite web |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/3260435/Stomach-stapled-MPs-put-weight-behind-Turia |title=Stomach-stapled MPs put weight behind Turia |author=Forbes, Michael |date=26 January 2010 |work=Stuff |location=New Zealand |access-date=16 September 2011}} Tolley joins other current and former New Zealand politicians including [[Rahui Katene]], [[David Lange]], [[Chester Borrows]], [[Donna Awatere-Huata]] and [[Tariana Turia]] to have had gastric bypass surgery at some point in the past. ==References== {{Reflist}}
